title: Overview and justification
body:
This course assumes you can already reference accurately and consistently, and that you already understand why academic work does so. What it adds is judgement under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role where getting it wrong has consequences beyond a lost mark.

By the end you will be able to justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression than the evidence supports, and act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work. You will also be able to respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Justify a course of action when a weak or disappointing result raises an ethical choice between honest reporting and presenting a stronger impression.
  • Justify acting to correct an unsupported figure or claim in shared work, upholding honesty even where the error would otherwise go unnoticed.
  • Justify a response to a fairness issue in shared work, weighing the discomfort of speaking up against the responsibility that courage requires.
  • Raise an unacknowledged contribution with those involved, treating them with respect, and help secure a fairer outcome even where the conversation is uncomfortable.
  • Critique your own habits of honesty and attribution against the ethical expectations of a profession, identifying where those expectations will tighten.
  • Recognise and act on an ethical responsibility in a new professional role without being asked, and explain the habit to someone newer than yourself.

title: In real academic practice
body: These are not abstract ethical puzzles. They are the situations that come up in a dissertation, a group project, a placement or a first professional role, where a weak result, an unattributed contribution, or an unfamiliar source type lands on your desk with no one checking your working. The judgement this course builds sits alongside your critical and research practice, informing the same honesty that underpins every claim you make and every source you cite elsewhere.

title: Signpost
body: The course has six short lessons, each built around a situation you might actually face. First, a weak result and the choice between honest reporting and a stronger impression. Second, correcting an unsupported claim in shared work. Third, a fairness issue in shared work. Fourth, raising an unacknowledged contribution. Fifth, weighing your own habits against a profession's expectations. Sixth, acting on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the six lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

I can justify acting to correct an unsupported figure or claim in shared work, even if the error would otherwise go unnoticed.

I can critique my own habits of honesty and attribution against the ethical expectations of a profession.

title: Orientation
body: Not every result comes out the way you hoped. A weak result, a null finding or a small effect size is not itself a problem: it is information. The problem arises in how you choose to report it, because a weak result creates a genuine temptation to describe it in terms stronger than the data support.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to recognise that temptation as an ethical choice, not a writing problem to be solved with better phrasing. The question is not how to make a weak result sound better; it is whether you report it as accurately as you would report a strong one.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Recognise an ethical choice raised by a weak result.
  • Classify a response to a weak result as honest or embellished.
  • Justify a course of action that reports a weak result honestly.

title: Concept: definition
body: An honest report of a weak result describes the outcome, including its limits, in the same terms you would use for a strong one. It uses no qualifier implying more certainty than the data support, omits nothing that complicates the narrative, and reframes no null or small effect as closer to significant than it was. Embellishment does not require a false statement; it is often achieved through selective emphasis, a softened verb, or a comparison chosen to flatter the result.

title: Concept: in practice
body: The temptation is strongest where the stakes feel highest. A dissertation result that falls short of what a supervisor expected, a pilot study that found no effect before a larger study is funded, or a project outcome due for assessment against peers whose results look stronger: each can trigger it. In each case the honest and the embellished report can describe the identical finding; the difference lies entirely in the language chosen around it.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now distinguished an honest report of a weak result from an embellished one. The habit to carry forward is treating every result the same way before you know how it will look. Decide how you would describe a strong result, and hold a weak one to that identical standard rather than reaching for softer language only when the data disappoint you.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time your own result, data or outcome was weaker than you hoped. How did you choose to describe it in writing? Looking back, would you call that description honest, embellished, or somewhere in between?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice the pressure before it shapes your next report.

title: Summary
body: A weak result is not itself a problem; the ethical choice lies in how you report it. You can now recognise that choice when it arises, and classify a given response as honest or as embellished even when no statement in it is technically false. You can also justify reporting a weak result in the same terms you would use for a strong one, as a professional default rather than a special favour to the data.

_items.title: See pages 185 to 187 of Chapter 10, 'Defining academic integrity', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course, and of this pathway. Referencing is no longer a mechanical or even a judgement skill: it is an ethical practice you can be trusted with. You can justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, and act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work. You can also respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved, and carry this judgement into whatever comes next in your own academic and professional practice.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, this is a habit you carry rather than a course you finish. Notice the moment a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, and choose honest reporting anyway. Notice an unsupported claim or an unacknowledged contribution in shared work, and act on it even when the conversation is uncomfortable. This same ethical attention underpins the arguments you build in your academic writing and the rigour you bring to researching and investigating. It also runs through the judgement you exercise whenever you read and evaluate critically: it is not a separate strand of your practice but the integrity running through all of them.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 185 to 187 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

body: Your results are weaker than expected. Reporting them honestly risks a less impressive outcome than quietly rounding the figures favourably. What justifies the honest choice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies reporting a weak result honestly?

_items.text: The report's value depends on it reflecting what was actually found, not how impressive it looks.
_items.feedback: Yes. A report is only useful if it reflects what was actually found, however it looks.

_items.text: Honesty is only required when someone is likely to check the figures.
_items.feedback: The obligation doesn't depend on the chance of being checked.

_items.text: Rounding the figures favourably is fine as long as the difference is small.
_items.feedback: A small difference still misrepresents what was actually found.

_items.text: A weaker result reflects badly on the student, so presentation should compensate.
_items.feedback: Compensating through presentation is exactly the choice the question asks you to justify against.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The report's value depends on reflecting what was actually found, whatever the result looks like.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Weigh what the report is for against how it might look to a reader.

body: You notice an unsupported figure in a piece of shared work that no one else has spotted. What justifies correcting it rather than leaving it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies correcting an unnoticed unsupported figure?

_items.text: Honesty in the work doesn't depend on whether an error would be noticed.
_items.feedback: Yes. The standard to meet is honesty in the work, not whether an error would be caught.

_items.text: It only needs correcting once someone else raises it as a problem.
_items.feedback: Waiting for someone else to raise it leaves the error standing in the meantime.

_items.text: Leaving it is acceptable since the rest of the work is otherwise strong.
_items.feedback: The strength of the rest of the work doesn't excuse an unsupported figure.

_items.text: Correcting it is only necessary if your own name is directly attached to that figure.
_items.feedback: Shared work carries a shared responsibility for its claims, not just the one attached to a figure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Honesty in shared work doesn't depend on whether an unsupported figure would otherwise go unnoticed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what honesty in the work requires, regardless of who might notice.

body: Raising a fairness issue in shared work means an uncomfortable conversation with people you work closely with. What justifies speaking up anyway?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies raising an uncomfortable fairness issue?

_items.text: The responsibility to address unfairness holds even when raising it is uncomfortable.
_items.feedback: Yes. The responsibility holds regardless of how comfortable raising it feels.

_items.text: Speaking up is only justified once the unfairness has caused visible harm.
_items.feedback: Waiting for visible harm means the unfairness continues in the meantime.

_items.text: Discomfort is a sign the issue probably isn't serious enough to raise.
_items.feedback: Discomfort reflects the conversation's difficulty, not the seriousness of the issue itself.

_items.text: It is someone else's responsibility to notice and raise it first.
_items.feedback: Responsibility for noticing an issue doesn't transfer to whoever speaks first.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The responsibility to address unfairness holds, even when the conversation is genuinely uncomfortable.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Weigh the discomfort against what the responsibility actually requires of you.

body: A contribution to shared work has gone unacknowledged. What does raising it with those involved, respectfully, aim to achieve?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does raising an unacknowledged contribution respectfully aim to achieve?

_items.text: A fairer outcome, reached without treating anyone involved with disrespect.
_items.feedback: Yes. The aim is a fairer outcome, reached in a way that respects everyone involved.

_items.text: An admission of fault, regardless of how the conversation is handled.
_items.feedback: Securing an admission isn't the goal; a fairer outcome, reached respectfully, is.

_items.text: A record that can be used if the issue needs escalating later.
_items.feedback: Building a record for later escalation isn't the stated aim of raising it now.

_items.text: A quick resolution, even if it leaves the underlying unfairness unaddressed.
_items.feedback: Speed at the expense of fairness misses the point of raising it at all.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The aim is a fairer outcome, reached without treating anyone involved with disrespect.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a fair and respectful outcome would actually look like here.

body: You compare your own habits of honesty and attribution against a profession's ethical expectations. What should that critique help you identify?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should critiquing your habits against a profession's expectations identify?

_items.text: Where those expectations will tighten beyond what is currently required of you.
_items.feedback: Yes. The critique should surface where the profession's expectations go further than your current habits.

_items.text: Whether your current habits already meet every expectation you might ever face.
_items.feedback: Confirming that everything already meets expectations misses where the gaps actually are.

_items.text: That professional expectations and academic ones are essentially the same.
_items.feedback: Treating them as the same overlooks exactly where they are likely to differ.

_items.text: That habits formed as a student need no further attention once qualified.
_items.feedback: Assuming no further attention is needed is the opposite of what a critique should surface.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The critique should identify where a profession's expectations will tighten beyond your current habits.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where the gap between your habits and the profession's standards is likely to appear.

body: In a new professional role, you notice an ethical responsibility that no one has asked you to take on. What does acting on it, and explaining it to someone newer, demonstrate?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does acting on and passing on an unprompted responsibility demonstrate?

_items.text: Recognising and acting on the responsibility without being prompted, and passing on the habit.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking it on unprompted and passing the habit on both demonstrate the same ethical habit.

_items.text: Waiting until someone senior confirms the responsibility is yours to take on.
_items.feedback: Waiting for confirmation is the opposite of acting without being asked.

_items.text: Treating the responsibility as optional until it appears in a formal role description.
_items.feedback: An ethical responsibility doesn't wait for a job description to make it count.

_items.text: Assuming someone newer will work it out for themselves in time.
_items.feedback: Leaving it to be worked out alone is the opposite of explaining the habit to them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Acting unprompted and explaining the habit to someone newer both show the responsibility has become genuinely yours.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what taking the responsibility on, and passing it on, actually requires of you.

title: Honest or embellished?
body: A pilot study found no significant difference between two teaching methods. For each way of describing this result, decide whether it is honest or embellished.
instruction: Match each description to the correct category.

_items.text: "The two methods produced no significant difference in outcomes."
"The results suggest a promising trend favouring the new method."
"The difference approached significance."
"This small pilot was not powered to detect a difference of this size, if one exists."

_feedback.correct: Notice that embellishment here never states a falsehood; it borrows the language of a positive finding for a result that was not one. That is exactly the choice this lesson asks you to recognise.

_incorrect.notFinal: Check whether the phrase would lead a reader to expect a stronger finding than the data actually show, even if no individual word in it is false.

title: From most honest to most embellished
displayTitle: From most honest to most embellished
body: A study found a small effect size that did not reach statistical significance. Order these five descriptions of that single result from most honest to most embellished.
instruction: Drag the descriptions into order, most honest first.

_items.text: "The effect did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.09)."
"A small effect was observed, though it did not reach conventional significance thresholds."
"The effect approached significance, indicating a likely true difference."
"Results support the hypothesis, with a positive effect observed across conditions."
"The hypothesis was confirmed by the data."

_feedback.correct: The honest end of this order states the exact statistic and lets it stand; the embellished end claims confirmation the data do not support. The middle positions are where most real embellishment happens, through softened language rather than outright claims.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh each description by what a reader would reasonably conclude from it, not by whether it contains a false statement. The most embellished option need not lie; it only needs to overstate.

title: Worked example: reporting a disappointing dissertation result

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: {{learner-a}}'s dissertation finds no significant relationship between the two variables under study. In the write-up, {{learner-a}} describes the result as "a trend in the expected direction that approached significance" and devotes most of the discussion to studies that found a positive effect, mentioning the null finding only briefly near the end.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} faces the identical null result. {{learner-b}} reports it plainly as no significant relationship, states the exact statistic, and discusses it with the same weight given to a positive result: considering what the null finding might mean for the underlying theory, and what a differently designed study might still find. The discussion is shorter than a positive result might have produced, but it represents the actual evidence rather than a more flattering version of it.

title: Four subtly embellished phrasings
body: Each phrase below could appear in a results section without an editor querying it. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see why it embellishes a weak result.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: "Trending towards significance"
_items.back: Statistically, a result either reached the chosen threshold or did not; no intermediate state exists. This phrase borrows the language of significance for a result that lacks it.

_items.title: "Broadly consistent with the hypothesis"
_items.back: "Broadly consistent" can describe almost any result that is not a clear contradiction, including a null one. It implies support that the data may not actually provide.

_items.title: "A promising direction for future research"
_items.back: This is often true and often honest, but it can also be used to reframe a disappointing result as an opportunity, quietly skipping over what the current data actually showed.

_items.title: "Results were in line with expectations"
_items.back: If the result was weaker than expected, this phrase misrepresents the comparison between what was predicted and what was found.

title: Why honest reporting of weak results matters
displayTitle: Why honest reporting of weak results matters
body: Expand each heading to see a consequence of embellishing a weak result.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: For anyone who builds on your work
_items.body: A researcher who later tries to replicate or extend an embellished finding is working from a false premise about how strong the original evidence was.

_items.title: For the field's evidence base
_items.body: Null and weak results that are reframed as positive distort the published record on a question, making the overall evidence look stronger than it is.

_items.title: For your own credibility
_items.body: A pattern of embellishment, once noticed by a supervisor or reviewer, affects how your future results are read, including the honest ones.

_items.title: For the decision the result informs
_items.body: If a weak result feeds into a real decision, such as whether to fund a larger study, an embellished description can lead to a decision the actual evidence does not support.

title: Heuristics for reporting a weak result honestly
displayTitle: Heuristics for reporting a weak result honestly
body:
These are checks to weigh against your own report, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Have you stated the exact statistic or outcome, rather than a qualitative phrase that could be read as stronger?
  • Would you have used this same language if the result had come out the way you hoped?
  • Have you avoided phrases that borrow the vocabulary of significance for a result that did not reach it?
  • Have you given the weak result the same discussion space you would give a strong one, rather than mentioning it briefly and moving on?
  • Have you disclosed any exclusions, subsets or reanalyses that make the result look better than the full data would?

title: Check 1
instruction: A student's experiment produces a much smaller effect than expected. Which best describes the ethical choice this raises?

_items.text: Whether to rerun the experiment until a larger effect appears.
Whether to describe the result in the same terms as a stronger result would warrant.
Whether the experiment was designed correctly.
Whether to include the result in the final report at all.

_feedback.correct: The ethical choice is not about the result itself, which cannot be changed, but about the language used to describe it: whether that language matches the data or borrows the vocabulary of a stronger finding.

_incorrect.notFinal: The result itself is already fixed by this point. Think about what decision remains open once the data are in.

title: Check 2
instruction: A results section describes a non-significant finding as "approaching significance and consistent with a true effect". What makes this description embellished rather than honest?

_items.text: It contains a factually false statistic.
It claims a degree of support for the hypothesis that the data did not reach.
It is too technical for a general reader to understand.
It omits the sample size used in the study.

_feedback.correct: Embellishment of this kind rarely depends on a false statistic. It depends on language that implies a stronger finding than the result actually supports, which is exactly what happened here.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look for whether any individual fact stated is false, or whether the overall impression the phrase creates goes beyond what the data show.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have a weak result to report in a piece of work for {{context}}. What is the strongest justification for reporting it honestly rather than in stronger terms?

_items.text: An honest report is easier to write than an embellished one.
An honest report holds the result to the same standard you would apply if it had turned out well, and keeps the evidence base reliable for anyone who builds on it.
Markers rarely read the results section closely enough to notice embellishment.
A weak result reported honestly will usually receive a higher mark than one reported in stronger terms.

_feedback.correct: The justification is not about ease, detection risk, or marks. It is that honest reporting applies one consistent standard regardless of outcome, and that anyone relying on your result later is relying on an accurate account of it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about why honest reporting matters even when nobody would notice the embellishment. The justification should hold regardless of who is checking.
